concept.name: National market system
concept.definition: The U.S. regulatory framework, mandated by Congress in Section 11A of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and implemented chiefly through Regulation NMS (2005), that links competing securities markets through consolidated data, order protection, and access rules. Its statutory objectives include efficient execution, fair competition among markets, price transparency, best execution, and interaction of investor orders.
concept.intuition: Congress decided stocks should trade on many competing venues but behave like one connected market, with shared prices and rules that stop your order from being filled at a worse price than displayed elsewhere.
concept.mechanics: Regulation NMS rules operationalize the mandate: Rule 611 (order protection/trade-through), Rule 610 (access), Rule 612 (minimum pricing increments), and Rules 601-603 (display and consolidated data dissemination through NMS plans such as CTA, UTP, and LULD).
concept.failure_modes: The NMS objectives conflict with each other — competition among venues fragments order flow and can weaken order interaction and public price discovery; the trade-through rule protects displayed prices that sophisticated traders can route around structurally.
concept.misconceptions: The NMS is not a single marketplace or system you can log into — it is a set of rules and linkages across venues — and 'best price' protection applies only to displayed, accessible quotations, not hidden or odd-lot interest.
concept.example: Because of Rule 611, an exchange generally cannot execute your buy order at $50.05 while another exchange displays an accessible offer at $50.00; the order must be routed to or priced through the better displayed quote.
